idiom_name: per-scope std::unordered_map plus a std::vector<Scope> as the open-scope stack (RAII scope guard)
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the container, not the pattern: the canonical realization is a Scope type holding std::unordered_map<std::string, Symbol> (or a pmr-aware map) with either a parent pointer or a std::vector<Scope> used as a cactus stack, plus define and lookup that walk outward from the innermost scope. What replaces the classic structure is the container plus RAII - a small scope-guard object pushes on construction and pops on destruction, keeping the stack discipline correct even when an exception unwinds through the resolver - and string interning (std::string_view keys into one owned unordered_set of identifier strings) removes repeated hashing of long names. Keep the hand-written table for compilers, DSLs and front ends; production toolchains do exactly this (GCC's name-lookup keeps scope stacks and binding tables by hand), while a scope-local std::map is preferable only when deterministic diagnostic order matters more than lookup speed.
pitfalls: Borrowing keys: std::string_view (or const char*) keys into a mutable source buffer dangle as soon as the buffer is freed or reallocated - intern into an owned arena or store std::string keys.

Scopes held by value in a growing std::vector move on reallocation, invalidating parent pointers and any symbol pointer handed out earlier; store scopes in an arena, use a stable container, or address them by index.
A hand-rolled push/pop leaks a scope when a resolver step throws or returns early - bind the push and pop into an RAII guard and never keep references into a scope the guard has popped.
